input.rationale: Interpreted the completed transfer probe for @transfer_nonvoter against its question: the call naming a non-voter reports success while the requested server never becomes leader and leadership moves to a later term (receipt b2c0026c56d54511999e5c37ef8372cd, parsed indices 0-3), with the voter-target control completing a real transfer. The account is now execution-backed, and the question's liveness half is recorded as partial because that receipt sampled leadership only at endpoints; a revised probe was built that samples every millisecond, records leaderless sample counts and the first and last leaderless millisecond, and asserts both that the previous leader was observed outside Leader state and that the cluster was observed with no leader at all. Its execution is requested as a revision of the same experiment. This update also answers both registered gaps with the partial progress available: no successor-overlap condition has been identified for @verify_quorum, and for @transfer_nonvoter the interruption is shown to occur but its length is still unmeasured.

interpretations.rationale: VerifyLeader's documented role is to ensure this peer is still the leader so that stale data is not returned from the FSM. The question was whether its success establishes voter-majority contact; the execution says it does not. In the retained run of the three-partition probe, the leader whose only reachable peer was the non-voter returned success in 0ms while its own latest configuration reported three voters, one non-voter and a quorum size of 2, and the leader was still in Leader state (parsed event index 1); the control partition that kept one voter reachable also returned success, which shows the harness does observe a genuine acknowledgement path (index 3); the control partition with no reachable peer did not return success at all, returning 'leadership lost while committing log' after 202ms with the node in Follower state, so the leader cannot reach the threshold on its own vote and the non-voter acknowledgement is what satisfied it in the first case (index 5). All three declared comparisons hold with the setup event matched as admission (correlations 1->0, 3->2, 5->4). The source explains the mechanism: verifyLeader asks every entry of leaderState.replState to acknowledge, startStopReplication creates such an entry for every configured server except the leader without consulting Suffrage, any successful AppendEntries or InstallSnapshot reply from such a peer calls notifyAll(true) and increments verifyFuture.votes, and the threshold compared against is quorumSize(), counted over voters alone. The same package treats voter eligibility strictly in its other leadership tests: checkLeaderLease does not count a non-voter, requestVote refuses a candidate that holds no vote, and quorumSize itself counts only voters, so the verify path is the outlier rather than a deliberate relaxation. The consequence for reads stays bounded and is not what this receipt measures. The leader's lease is voter-only, and both Config.Validate and ReloadConfig enforce LeaderLeaseTimeout <= HeartbeatTimeout <= ElectionTimeout, so the old leader is normally removed before a voter majority elects a successor; the no-peer control is exactly that lease firing at 202ms with a 200ms lease. What the receipt does establish is the weaker but unconditional part: for an interval in which the leader exchanged nothing with any other voter, VerifyLeader reports success, so a caller relying on that call for read consistency is really relying on the lease timer rather than on the acknowledgements VerifyLeader collected.

d704b04e706144dc964ff451359eda19-gap-0.explanation: Partial progress only. The receipt for this question did not witness a successor being elected while the old leader verified: in the non-voter partition the other servers stayed in term 2 with no leader change and the leader was still Leader at the endpoint. The two configuration routes that could stretch the old leader's mandate past a follower's election timer are closed by source: checkLeaderLease counts voters only, and ReloadConfig re-runs ValidateConfig so LeaderLeaseTimeout <= HeartbeatTimeout <= ElectionTimeout holds on a running node. What remains to be shown is a leader-side timing condition - a stall or clock jump longer than ElectionTimeout minus LeaderLeaseTimeout, or a verify request admitted before the ready lease case - and no legal instance has been identified.

counterevidence: checkLeaderLease counts voters only, so a leader that has lost voter-majority contact steps down within about LeaderLeaseTimeout; the no-peer control shows this concretely (leadership lost at 202ms with a 200ms lease), which bounds the stale-read consequence rather than showing the verify decision support to be adequate.

Config.Validate keeps LeaderLeaseTimeout <= HeartbeatTimeout <= ElectionTimeout, and ReloadConfig re-runs ValidateConfig, so a leader cannot be configured to outlive a follower's election timer through the public reload API.

In the non-voter partition the other servers stayed in term 2 with no leader change, so the receipt does not witness a successor being elected while the old leader still verified; that half of the consequence remains unobserved.
limitations: The stale-read consequence still needs a successor elected while the old leader reports verify success, for example a leader-side stall or clock jump longer than ElectionTimeout - LeaderLeaseTimeout, or a verify request served before a ready lease case; the registered gap tracks that search and is not resolved by this receipt.

The probe uses one process with real Raft instances and in-memory transports, so it exercises the leader's own replication and verify paths but not process-level partitions or multi-host clocks; the partition was made by disconnecting transports in both directions.
One execution of each case is cited; repeatability of the timing-sensitive control (the 202ms lease step-down) is not established.

interpretations.rationale: The question was whether LeadershipTransferToServer reports a transfer that the named server can complete when that server is a non-voter, and what happens to leadership while it cannot. The execution answers the first half directly. In the control case naming a voter (parsed indices 0 and 1) the call returned nil and the requested server was Leader at the endpoint while the previous leader was Follower, so the call does perform real transfers. In the case naming the non-voter (parsed indices 2 and 3, setup event index 2 matched as admission) the same call returned nil while the requested server was never observed as Leader within 1500ms and finished as Follower; the previous leader was not Leader at the endpoint and the maximum term across the cluster had risen from 2 to 4, with the same server holding leadership at term 4, which a Raft leader cannot do without having stepped down and won a later election. The source explains the mechanism as predicted. The leader resolves the requested ID only through leaderState.replState, which startStopReplication populates for every configured server except the leader without consulting Suffrage, so a non-voter passes and receives TimeoutNow; timeoutNow sets it to Candidate and marks candidateFromLeadershipTransfer, a flag that by design suppresses pre-vote, so it sends a real RequestVote carrying the next term. Each voter adopts the higher term and becomes a follower before reaching the hasVote check, which then refuses the vote because the candidate holds no vote, so the requested server can never collect a grant. The old leader learns of the higher term, steps down, and its transfer goroutine reports success from the leftLeaderLoop branch, so the caller is told the transfer succeeded while leadership has in fact left it for a server it did not choose, or returned to it in a later term. That mismatch is the defect: for the documented purpose of handing leadership over, a success result that the named target can never satisfy leaves the caller unable to distinguish a completed handover from a self-inflicted leadership interruption. The liveness side is bounded rather than unbounded and this receipt does not measure it, since leadership was sampled only at the end of the observation window; the revised probe samples every millisecond and records the leaderless samples. No data loss is claimed: committed entries stay committed and a voter is elected afterwards.

627b3ef0c6e049bfb836e40ffbdce875-gap-1.explanation: Partial progress. The execution shows the previous leader does not keep leadership: in the non-voter case it was not Leader at the endpoint and the cluster's maximum term had risen from 2 to 4 with the same server holding leadership at term 4, which a leader cannot do without having stepped down and won a later election. The leaderless interval itself is not bounded by that receipt, because leadership was only sampled when the returned result and the 1500ms target window ended. The revised probe submitted here samples leadership every millisecond and records leaderless sample counts, the first and last leaderless millisecond, and how often the previous leader was seen outside Leader state.

counterevidence: The API comment does not state that the target must be a voter, and a caller who names only voters never reaches this path, so the defect depends on an accepted calling pattern rather than on the library's own choice of target.

LeadershipTransfer() without an explicit target filters non-voters in pickServer, which shows the intended transfer target set is the voter set and supports reading the targeted call as requiring the same premise.
A TimeoutNow that cannot be delivered (unreachable target) is reported as an error by the transfer path, so not every unusable target is silently accepted.

The interruption is bounded: the remaining voters re-elect after their election timers, and the control case shows the probe does observe a completed transfer, so the outcome is a wrong success report and a leadership interruption rather than a cluster that never recovers.
limitations: Whether the call reports success and the requested target cannot win rests on one execution per case (receipt b2c0026c56d54511999e5c37ef8372cd, indices 0-3); the identity of the leader after the interruption is timing dependent and is only recorded, not asserted.

The leaderless interval is not bounded by this receipt: leadership state was sampled once after the returned result and after a 1500ms wait, so no interval measurement exists yet; the revised probe with 1ms sampling is submitted for that.
The claim concerns the reported result of the call, the requested target's inability to win and the observed leadership change; it does not assert data loss.
The probe uses one process with real Raft instances and in-memory transports, so it exercises the leader's own transfer, election and vote paths but not process-level partitions or multi-host clocks.

scope.description: Observe both halves of a leadership transfer request naming a non-voter: what LeadershipTransferToServer reports, which server actually holds leadership, and how the cluster's leadership state evolves during the attempt, sampled every millisecond, with the same call naming a voter as the control. Each case emits an assurance_transfer_target setup event and an assurance_transfer_result event carrying the returned result, the target and previous-leader states, leader sets and terms, and the sampling counters.
assumptions: Three voters plus one non-voter is a supported configuration; the non-voter is joined through the leader's own AddNonvoter call.
HeartbeatTimeout = ElectionTimeout = LeaderLeaseTimeout = 200ms and CommitTimeout = 5ms satisfy Config.Validate, and protocol version >= 3 supports LeadershipTransferToServer.
A voter target is a legal and expected use, so the voter case is the control that the probe can observe a completed transfer.

Sampling every millisecond is fine-grained relative to the 200ms election timeout, so a leaderless interval lasting an election round is expected to be visible; shorter gaps are not bounded by this sampling rate.
excluded: Process-level stalls, host suspends and multi-host clock behaviour, which a single-process in-memory probe does not reproduce.

experiment.prefix: Each case builds four real Raft instances in one process with their own InmemStore, InmemSnapshotStore and InmemTransport, fully connected before any node starts. Three voters are bootstrapped with BootstrapCluster as Voter; the fourth node is started without a configuration and joined through the elected leader's own AddNonvoter(id, address, 0, 5s) call, waiting until the leader's latest configuration reports it. The target is chosen by configuration role, never by a measured result: the first voter that is not the leader as the control, the joined non-voter as the probe; its suffrage is read from the leader's latest configuration and emitted in the setup event. The case calls leader.LeadershipTransferToServer(target.id, target.addr) and, from that instant, a goroutine samples every millisecond whether any of the four nodes is in Leader state and whether the previous leader is outside Leader state. It waits up to 5s for the returned result, up to 1500ms for the requested target to be observed as Leader, then records the leader set, the maximum term, whether the term rose above the pre-call term, and the sampling counters. Both cases share the harness TestAssuranceLeadershipTransferTarget under distinct case names.

comparisons.description: Non-voter target: what the call reported. Holds means the predicted success report was observed, which supports the defect account rather than contradicting it.
Non-voter target: the requested server never became leader within the observation window.
Non-voter target: the previous leader was sampled outside Leader state during the attempt, so it did give up leadership.
Non-voter target: at least one sample found no leader in the cluster, with the first and last leaderless millisecond recorded alongside.
Voter target control: the same call does transfer leadership, so the non-voter outcome is not a probe that never transfers.
Voter target control: the reported result for a transfer that does complete.

experiment.revision_reason: The previous run of this harness answered the reported-result half of the question but sampled leadership state only at endpoints, so it could not say whether the cluster was ever without a leader or for how long. This revision adds a 1ms sampling goroutine running from the transfer call until after the observation window, reporting leaderless sample counts, the first and last leaderless millisecond, how often the previous leader was seen outside Leader state, and the endpoint leader identity, with two comparisons asserting those observations for the non-voter case. Measured result fields, cases and target selection are unchanged.

scope.description: Observe VerifyLeader's returned endpoint at the leader of a four-server cluster (three voters plus one non-voter) after partitioning the leader away from the voter majority, comparing a partition that keeps only the non-voter reachable, one that keeps one voter reachable, and one that keeps no peer reachable. Each case emits one CA_EVENT with the leader ID and address, the voters and non-voters read from the leader's latest configuration, the quorum size, the leader term, the other servers' terms and states, the leader's state after the call, the VerifyLeader result and the elapsed time.

basis.prefix: Each case builds four real Raft instances in one process, each with its own InmemStore, InmemSnapshotStore and InmemTransport; the transports are fully connected before any node is started. The three voters are bootstrapped with BootstrapCluster from a configuration naming all three as Voter; the fourth node is started without a configuration and joined through the elected leader's own AddNonvoter(id, address, 0, 5s) call, and the case waits until the leader's latest configuration reports the non-voter before proceeding. Configuration: HeartbeatTimeout = ElectionTimeout = LeaderLeaseTimeout = 200ms, CommitTimeout = 5ms, default ProtocolVersion, which satisfies Config.Validate. After a 300ms settling period the transports are disconnected in both directions across the chosen boundary, so only the listed peers remain reachable from the leader; the observation then calls VerifyLeader() on the leader and reports nil, a concrete error, or pending after a 900ms wait. The peer kept reachable as a voter is chosen by position in the bootstrap configuration, and the non-voter by its join identity, never by a measured result.

Disconnecting both directions across the partition boundary models a network split rather than closing a node, so the leader keeps running and its lease timer still fires.

The source trace shows the guarantee is weaker than that role requires: the confirming votes are gathered from every replication peer, including non-voters, while the threshold is a voter quorum. With three voters and one non-voter, quorumSize() is 2, so the leader's own vote plus a single non-voter acknowledgement reaches the threshold and VerifyLeader returns nil; the same code gives the non-voter no standing in checkLeaderLease's lease count or in a vote request, so the two leadership tests disagree about whose support counts. Config.Validate keeps LeaderLeaseTimeout <= HeartbeatTimeout <= ElectionTimeout, and ReloadConfig re-runs ValidateConfig, so a leader cannot be configured to outlive a follower's election timer through the public reload API.

In the non-voter partition the other servers stayed in term 2 with no leader change, so the receipt does not witness a successor being elected while the old leader still verified; that half of the consequence remains unobserved.
limitations: The stale-read consequence still needs a successor elected while the old leader reports verify success, for example a leader-side stall or clock jump longer than ElectionTimeout - LeaderLeaseTimeout, or a verify request served before a ready lease case; the registered gap tracks that search and is not resolved by this receipt.

The probe uses one process with real Raft instances and in-memory transports, so it exercises the leader's own replication and verify paths but not process-level partitions or multi-host clocks; the partition was made by disconnecting transports in both directions.
One execution of each case is cited; repeatability of the timing-sensitive control (the 202ms lease step-down) is not established.

interpretations.rationale: The documented purpose of LeadershipTransferToServer is to transition leadership to a specific server in the cluster, and the only target validation in the leader is a lookup in leaderState.replState, which holds an entry for every configured server except the leader regardless of Suffrage; a missing entry is the sole error. A non-voter therefore passes validation and is sent TimeoutNow, which makes it a Candidate with candidateFromLeadershipTransfer set, a flag that by design suppresses pre-vote so the node sends a real RequestVote with a higher term. Voters processing that request adopt the higher term and set themselves to Follower before the hasVote check rejects the candidate, so the candidate cannot collect a single grant, while the old leader loses leadership because it adopts the higher term too and its transfer goroutine then reports success from the leftLeaderLoop branch. The account is asserted on that source basis and stays conditional until the requested two-case probe reports what the call returns versus which server actually takes leadership; the controlling contrast is the same call naming a voter, and the note that auto-targeted LeadershipTransfer() skips non-voters via pickServer shows the library itself does not consider a non-voter a valid transfer target when it chooses.
counterevidence: The API does not state in its comment that the target must be a voter, and a caller who names only voters never reaches this path, so the defect depends on an accepted calling pattern rather than on the library's own choice of target.

LeadershipTransfer() without an explicit target filters non-voters in pickServer, which shows the intended transfer target set is the voter set and supports reading the targeted call as requiring the same premise.
A TimeoutNow that cannot be delivered (unreachable target) is reported as an error by the transfer path, so not every unusable target is silently accepted.
limitations: No receipt exists yet for this question; the harness for the two-case probe is submitted with this update and its outcome is predicted, not observed.

Whether the cluster is briefly leaderless after the non-voter's campaign, and for how long, is registered as a gap: the current probe samples leadership state at the end of a 1500ms window, which is too coarse to bound a leaderless interval.
The claim concerns the reported result of the call and the requested target's inability to win; it does not assert data loss, since committed entries remain committed and a fresh election follows.

result.summary: Interpreted the transfer receipt (b2c0026c56d54511999e5c37ef8372cd, parsed indices 0-3): naming a voter, the call returned nil and the requested server ended as Leader with the previous leader Follower; naming the non-voter, the same call returned nil while the requested server was never Leader in a 1500ms window, finished Follower, and the cluster's maximum term rose 2 to 4 with the same server leading at term 4 — so the handover reported as successful never reached the named target. The question account is now 'explained' with the source mechanism (target resolved through replState, TimeoutNow, pre-vote skipped, voters adopting the higher term then rejecting the vote, old leader's goroutine reporting success from leftLeaderLoop). Both registered gaps are now answered with partial progress and left unresolved, and I revised the probe to bound the liveness half: a 1ms sampling goroutine records leaderless sample counts, the first and last leaderless millisecond, and how often the previous leader was outside Leader state, with two new comparisons asserting those observations; its execution is requested as a revision of the same experiment. scope.description: Observe VerifyLeader's returned endpoint at the leader of a four-server cluster (three voters plus one non-voter) after partitioning the leader away from the voter majority, comparing a partition that keeps only the non-voter reachable, one that keeps one voter reachable, and one that keeps no peer reachable. Each case emits one CA_EVENT with the leader ID and address, the voters and non-voters read from the leader's latest configuration, the quorum size, the leader term, the other servers' terms and states, the leader's state after the call, the VerifyLeader result and the elapsed time.

basis.prefix: Each case builds four real Raft instances in one process, each with its own InmemStore, InmemSnapshotStore and InmemTransport; the transports are fully connected before any node is started. The three voters are bootstrapped with BootstrapCluster from a configuration naming all three as Voter; the fourth node is started without a configuration and joined through the elected leader's own AddNonvoter(id, address, 0, 5s) call, and the case waits until the leader's latest configuration reports the non-voter before proceeding. Configuration: HeartbeatTimeout = ElectionTimeout = LeaderLeaseTimeout = 200ms, CommitTimeout = 5ms, default ProtocolVersion, which satisfies Config.Validate. After a 300ms settling period the transports are disconnected in both directions across the chosen boundary, so only the listed peers remain reachable from the leader; the observation then calls VerifyLeader() on the leader and reports nil, a concrete error, or pending after a 900ms wait. The peer kept reachable as a voter is chosen by position in the bootstrap configuration, and the non-voter by its join identity, never by a measured result.

scope.description: Observe what LeadershipTransferToServer reports against which server actually takes leadership when the requested target is a non-voter, with the same call naming a voter as the only difference. basis.prefix: Each case builds four real Raft instances in one process, each with its own InmemStore, InmemSnapshotStore and InmemTransport, fully connected before any node starts. experiments.revision_reason: The previous run of this harness answered the reported-result half of the question but sampled leadership state only at endpoints, so it could not say whether the cluster was ever without a leader or for how long. This revision adds a 1ms sampling goroutine running from the transfer call until after the observation window, reporting leaderless sample counts, the first and last leaderless millisecond, how often the previous leader was seen outside Leader state, and the endpoint leader identity, with two comparisons asserting those observations for the non-voter case. interpretations.rationale: VerifyLeader's documented role is to ensure this peer is still the leader so that stale data is not returned from the FSM. The source trace shows the guarantee is weaker than that role requires: the confirming votes are gathered from every replication peer, including non-voters, while the threshold is a voter quorum. With three voters and one non-voter, quorumSize() is 2, so the leader's own vote plus a single non-voter acknowledgement reaches the threshold and VerifyLeader returns nil; the same code gives the non-voter no standing in checkLeaderLease's lease count or in a vote request, so the two leadership tests disagree about whose support counts. The consequence for reads is bounded rather than unconditional: checkLeaderLease uses voters only, so under a validated configuration the lease normally removes the old leader before a voter majority can elect a successor, and the acknowledgements counted while the leader is still legitimately leader are not themselves stale. The account therefore asserts a defect in the decision support VerifyLeader provides (success without voter-majority acknowledgement) and treats the stale-read consequence as conditional on the lease's timing assumption (a leader stall, clock jump or lease check interleaving that lets a successor be elected while the old leader still reports success). The requested probe fixes the acknowledging peer's identity independently of the result: the partition, not the outcome, selects the peer, and the non-voter is joined through the leader's own AddNonvoter path.
counterevidence: checkLeaderLease counts voters only, so a leader that has lost voter-majority contact steps down within about LeaderLeaseTimeout; this bounds the stale-read consequence rather than showing VerifyLeader's decision support to be adequate.

Config.Validate keeps LeaderLeaseTimeout <= HeartbeatTimeout <= ElectionTimeout, so a follower's election timer normally fires no earlier than the lease that causes the old leader to step down; the new-leader half of a stale read is therefore usually prevented by the lease rather than by the verify quorum.
limitations: The account is currently source-based; the three-case probe is requested with the recorded prediction that the non-voter-only partition returns success while the no-reachable-peer partition does not, and its retained receipt and parsed indices will be cited in a later update.
The probe uses one process with real Raft instances and in-memory transports, so it exercises the leader's own replication and verify paths but not process-level partitions or multi-host clocks.

interpretations.rationale: VerifyLeader's documented role is to ensure this peer is still the leader so that stale data is not returned from the FSM, and the question asks whether its success establishes the voter-majority contact that role implies. The source trace says no: verifyLeader registers every entry of leaderState.replState, which startStopReplication creates for every configured server except the leader without consulting Suffrage, so non-voters are asked to acknowledge; any successful AppendEntries or InstallSnapshot reply from such a peer calls notifyAll(true) and increments verifyFuture.votes, while the threshold compared against is quorumSize(), counted over voters alone. With three voters and one non-voter the threshold is 2, so the leader's own vote plus the non-voter's acknowledgement is a success. The same package treats voter eligibility strictly everywhere else: checkLeaderLease does not count a non-voter in its contacted tally, requestVote refuses a candidate that has no vote, and quorumSize itself counts voters only, so the verify path is the odd one out rather than a deliberate relaxation. The consequence for reads is bounded, not unconditional. Under a validated configuration the leader's lease is also voter-only and normally removes the old leader before a voter majority can elect a successor, and ReloadConfig re-validates the bounds at runtime, so a leader cannot be given a lease longer than a follower's election timeout. What remains unconditionally wrong is narrower and still real for a caller: VerifyLeader returns success for an interval in which the leader has exchanged nothing with any other voter, and the guarantee a client actually relies on is then being carried by the lease timer instead of by the acknowledgements VerifyLeader collected. The requested probe fixes the acknowledging peer's identity independently of the outcome: the partition selects which peer stays reachable, case identity is the case name and leader ID, and the non-voter is joined through the leader's own AddNonvoter path. Each case now emits a placement event before the partition and a result event after it, so the result comparison's admission cannot be the result event itself.

interpretations.rationale: The question was whether LeadershipTransferToServer reports a transfer that the named server can complete when that server is a non-voter, and what happens to leadership while it cannot. The execution answers the first half directly. In the control case naming a voter (parsed indices 0 and 1) the call returned nil and the requested server was Leader at the endpoint while the previous leader was Follower, so the call does perform real transfers. In the case naming the non-voter (parsed indices 2 and 3, setup event index 2 matched as admission) the same call returned nil while the requested server was never observed as Leader within 1500ms and finished as Follower; the previous leader was not Leader at the endpoint and the maximum term across the cluster had risen from 2 to 4, with the same server holding leadership at term 4, which a Raft leader cannot do without having stepped down and won a later election. The source explains the mechanism as predicted. The leader resolves the requested ID only through leaderState.replState, which startStopReplication populates for every configured server except the leader without consulting Suffrage, so a non-voter passes and receives TimeoutNow; timeoutNow sets it to Candidate and marks candidateFromLeadershipTransfer, a flag that by design suppresses pre-vote, so it sends a real RequestVote carrying the next term. Each voter adopts the higher term and becomes a follower before reaching the hasVote check, which then refuses the vote because the candidate holds no vote, so the requested server can never collect a grant. The old leader learns of the higher term, steps down, and its transfer goroutine reports success from the leftLeaderLoop branch, so the caller is told the transfer succeeded while leadership has in fact left it for a server it did not choose, or returned to it in a later term. That mismatch is the defect: for the documented purpose of handing leadership over, a success result that the named target can never satisfy leaves the caller unable to distinguish a completed handover from a self-inflicted leadership interruption. The liveness side is bounded rather than unbounded and this receipt does not measure it, since leadership was sampled only at the end of the observation window; the revised probe samples every millisecond and records the leaderless samples. No data loss is claimed: committed entries stay committed and a voter is elected afterwards.
